title: How to Keep AI-Generated Code Quality High Without Adding Reviewers

verdict.reason: Despite the vendor pitch at the end, the first half teaches product-independent techniques the card reports accurately: sorting the last 100 review comments into rule-checkable, testable and judgment buckets, negative acceptance criteria, and diffing tests for weakened assertions. It stays at 6 because evidence is thin, with no code or before-and-after.

title: Claude Reviewing Claude: Anthropic's Code Review Process Has No Second Model

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete cross-model review layer: a second lab's model reviews the diff and the host agent verifies findings, about 1 in 4 of which were wrong, with round caps and incident-based reviewer evals, backed by personal log numbers and specific caught bugs, though the evidence is admittedly rough and has no code or repo.

title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary

verdict.reason: This is mainly a Meta-scale privacy-infrastructure deep dive, with only a few paragraphs on agents. The card wrongly frames PrivacyLib as built for agents, and its 'steal this' carries the simulation-replay and percentage-rollout patterns over to agent tool permissions, which the page never applies them to, leaving nothing an engineer could realistically copy this week without comparable infrastructure.

title: Why Agents Love Supabase

verdict.reason: This is a podcast write-up of Supabase product announcements (Docker-free local runtime, declarative schemas, Compute alpha), so it amounts to launch news and vendor features; the page names the declarative-schema idea but never shows how to set it up or what changes in an agent's loop.

title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands

verdict.reason: The brain-versus-hands split (persistent harness, disposable sandboxes, credentials attached via a proxy) is described only at a conceptual level inside a long, mostly IPO- and launch-focused podcast, and Anthropic's own linked write-up covers it in more depth, so this is a thin rehash with no implementation detail to copy.

title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?

verdict.reason: This is mainly an opinion essay on why senior developers are cautious. The 'encode lessons into the harness' idea is mentioned only in passing, with no concrete files, checks or before/after, and the article admits the red-build problem it raises is unsolved, so there is no technique an engineer could copy this week.

title: How Anthropic ships the #1 LLM in the World safely: Separating the Brain from the Hands

verdict.reason: The page is a podcast landing page with only show notes and timestamps, with no transcript content teaching the brain/hand/sandbox split. The card's mechanics are inferred from link titles rather than taught on the page, and the episode leans heavily on launch and S-1 news.

title: Skills & Progressive Disclosure

verdict.reason: It teaches a concrete, copyable pattern: cut the always-loaded agent definition to identity, scope and a skill index, and move procedures into self-contained SKILL.md files loaded per task. It includes an example index, token arithmetic and named failure modes (index rot, wrong skill, hidden dependencies), but the numbers are illustrative rather than a measured before and after.

title: Elegance and intelligence are anticorrelated

verdict.reason: This is an opinion essay on intelligence and elegance with no concrete technique, and the card's 'ask the agent to refactor into abstractions' advice is invented rather than taught by the page.

title: Fragments: October 28

verdict.reason: This is a link-roundup of commentary, and the Vella section offers a conceptual framework (direct vs supervisory control, Endsley-Kiris autonomy levels) rather than a concrete technique; the card's 'pick an autonomy level and write down independent evidence to check' step is extrapolated, not something the page teaches.

title: An agent PR that only says 'fixed' makes the reviewer redo the diagnosis

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable technique: an evidence-based agent PR template (repro command, before/after check, scope, assumptions, revert) wired into the done-checklist, plus a cheap 'paste the failing log line' check, but it's short and has no real example template, repo or before/after.

title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here's Why.

verdict.reason: The essay is mostly analysis of why models succeed at math, but it does teach a transferable drafter/solver/verifier loop: fold each failed attempt back into the next prompt as a negative hint and promote known failure modes to standing adversarial checks, backed by the quoted CDC prompt. The setup is the author's reconstruction of what OpenAI likely did, not a demonstrated harness, so the technique is thin.

title: Building Conversational Commerce with Multi-Agent Swarms on GCP: A Working Prototype

verdict.reason: The page teaches transferable harness patterns: deterministic tools for pricing math (calculate_cart_totals), state kept outside the model in Redis, a cheap supervisor routing to small specialist prompts, and masked payment labels, all backed by code and test output; but the core idea is familiar and the piece is heavy on GCP infrastructure, so it's thin as a teaching item.

title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU

verdict.reason: This is a launch announcement for TPU inference engines with benchmark and leaderboard claims, so it is an automatic fail; prefix caching is serving infrastructure, not a transferable harness technique for getting verified agent output.

title: Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud

verdict.reason: The portable idea is a gate on agent-written code: an AST check, an OPA threshold check and human sign-off for structural changes. But the page is mostly Google Cloud product marketing (Model Armor, KMS, Binary Authorization) around a simulated demo, and it explains the gates only at a high level with no code on the page.

title: Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents

verdict.reason: This is a co-branded vendor tutorial for wiring A2UI into CopilotKit, and its key mechanics are product features rather than techniques the page teaches you to build. The sub-agent generation and self-healing retries come built into AG-UI integrations, and the component allowlist only works through their stack.

title: Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond

verdict.reason: This is mainly a product feature walkthrough for Google's Agents CLI Extension System, and the override, lockfile and recursion-guard mechanics only work inside that tool; the card's generic advice to wrap deploy in a script contradicts the article, which says agents bypass plain wrappers, and the clear-refusal idea is too thin to carry it.

title: Context Engineering Starts with Retrieval

verdict.reason: Teaches a transferable 'retrieve, offload, delegate' pattern with working code: a retrieval tool writes hits to files and returns only paths, and per-file subagents return key facts with sources; it docks for being framed around LangChain's Deep Agents harness, though the pattern ports to any harness.

title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec

verdict.reason: This is a product launch announcement for a Google Cloud API Gateway streaming feature, and its only 'technique' is a vendor-specific gcloud flag and model-routing feature, not a transferable agent-harness practice an engineer could copy elsewhere.

title: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK

verdict.reason: The page teaches a concrete tool-design pattern with code and a before-and-after benchmark (14.4s to 1.2s): switch slow tools to async generators that stream progress, pick a delivery mode (WHEN_IDLE, INTERRUPT, SILENT), and add a single-call latch and a stop_streaming cancel, but it is narrow and tied to Google's ADK and Gemini Live, which caps the score.

title: Give a coding-agent delivery enough evidence to review

verdict.reason: The page gives a copyable delivery template (reproduce command, baseline, after output, known limits, requested decision) and a rule to match each piece of evidence to the claim it supports, though it is AI-assisted vendor-adjacent content with only a toy fixture, and it frames the executor as a teammate optionally using an agent rather than the agent itself.

title: How We Built Our Design Agent

verdict.reason: The page walks through a working harness and what broke along the way, and its techniques transfer beyond the vendor's product: a router skill, code gates for order-critical steps, async subagents with ownership briefs, and AGENTS.md memory capped at 200 lines. It backs this with an open-source repo, though the 'real-setups' theme fits better than 'non-engineers'.

title: Your AI Agent Says “Done.” What Did It Actually Verify?

verdict.reason: Teaches a concrete, copyable technique: upfront observable acceptance criteria plus a reusable completion-report prompt (exact checks run, fail-first regression test, test-edit disclosure, unverified list), and the card accurately reflects the page, though the evidence is a small illustrative example rather than a real repo or before-and-after.

title: You can just ask AI to do things

verdict.reason: An engineer's actual daily harness with copyable techniques, such as having an agent poll logs and metrics before and after deploys, running curl happy paths against the dev server, getting second opinions from other models via subagents, and a scheduled 6am triage job; each is only lightly explained, with no code or before-and-after evidence.

title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO

verdict.reason: This is mostly a business interview about GPU economics; the snapshot-then-fork CI idea is only a wished-for future capability with no mechanics, and the sandbox-escape and agent-ranking ideas are passing mentions, so there is no concrete technique to copy this week.

title: The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute

verdict.reason: This is a podcast about GPU compute markets and physical settlement with no agent harness technique; the card's 'steal this' stretches an order-book matching idea into agent workflow design that the page never teaches, and even its own 'go deeper' line admits there is no agent technique.

title: How Numan Built an Eval-First AI Health Coach with LangGraph and LangSmith

verdict.reason: Despite being a LangChain case study, it teaches transferable eval techniques: per-category judge scoring instead of averages, a cheaper model playing a persona-driven simulated user against the real agent, evals run through the production graph, and safety probes that block releases. It loses points because evidence is qualitative, with no code, rubric samples or before-and-after numbers.

title: mattpocock/skills

verdict.reason: The repo provides copyable, editable skill files that the card describes accurately: grilling interviews, a GLOSSARY.md shared language with ADRs, TDD red-green-refactor loops, a gated bug-diagnosis loop and two-axis parallel sub-agent code review, all backed by real code and a before/after example; it is better filed under harness design than real setups.

title: 90% of my coding agent's rework came from my own work orders

verdict.reason: It teaches a concrete pre-handoff 'falsifier' pass, run twice, that turns up gaps in the work order. Each finding is ranked, quotes the triggering line and gives a breaking input. The evidence is a rework-sorting analysis (55 of 61 must-fix items came from the order) and measured catch rates, though the actual prompt isn't published and the sample is small.

title: Managed Deep Agents v0.10: Browser Use and Async Subagents

verdict.reason: This is a product release announcement for LangChain's Managed Deep Agents v0.10, and its techniques (the async: True subagent flag, browser_handoff) only work inside the vendor's platform, so it falls under the launch-news and vendor-marketing automatic fails despite the sound underlying patterns.
